title: Design a URL shortener
summary: A full design worked from requirements: estimates, the API, generating short keys, storing them, fast redirects and click counts.

blocks.p: Build a service that turns a long URL into a short one, such as `short.example/aZ3kP9q`, and sends anyone who opens the short link to the long URL.

list: **Create.** Given a long URL, return a short link. Links are kept for 5 years.
**Redirect.** Opening a short link redirects to the long URL, fast, from anywhere.
**Count clicks.** Owners can see how many times each link was opened.
**Scale.** 100 million new links a month. Links are read about 100 times as often as they are created.

blocks.p: Short keys shouldn't be guessable in order, so nobody can list every link by counting. Redirects matter most: a slow or failed redirect breaks a link someone shared.
Start with rough numbers, as in the estimates lesson. They decide which parts need care.

blocks.caption: Traffic and storage from the requirements. Writes are modest. Reads and total rows are what need planning.

blocks.p: About 40 writes a second is easy for one database. About 4,000 reads a second on average, with peaks several times higher, calls for a cache. Six billion rows over 5 years, a few terabytes, is more than one machine should hold comfortably, so plan to shard.

blocks.code:
POST /links
{ "url": "https://example.com/a/very/long/path?with=params" }

201 Created
{ "key": "aZ3kP9q", "short": "https://short.example/aZ3kP9q" }

GET /aZ3kP9q

302 Found
Location: https://example.com/a/very/long/path?with=params
Cache-Control: no-store
blocks.caption: Creating a link, and following it.

blocks.p: `301 Moved Permanently` lets browsers cache the redirect by default, so repeat clicks never reach you. That saves load but loses click counts, and makes changing where a link points hard once cached. `302 Found` is not cached by default, though browsers and proxies may still cache it if headers allow. With click counts as a requirement, use 302 and send `Cache-Control: no-store` so every click comes back to the service.
Keys use the 62 characters `a-z`, `A-Z` and `0-9`, called base62. Each extra character multiplies the number of keys by 62.

blocks.caption: How many keys a length gives, and how full the space is after 5 years at 100 million links a month.

blocks.p: Seven characters give about 3.5 trillion keys. After 5 years, 6 billion are used, under 0.2% of the space. There are three common ways to pick a key.

list: **Hash the URL.** Hash the long URL, encode the bytes in base62, and take the first 7 characters. Different URLs can still produce the same 7 characters, so you must check for collisions anyway.

**Count.** Give each link the next number from a counter and write it in base62. No collisions, but keys come out in order and can be guessed. One shared counter is also a hot spot. Handing each server a block of a thousand numbers at a time fixes the hot spot but not the guessing.
**Random.** Pick 7 random characters and insert with a unique constraint on the key. If the key exists, which happens to fewer than 1 insert in 500 even after 5 years, pick again.

blocks.p: Random keys meet every requirement: they are unguessable, need no coordination, and the database enforces uniqueness.

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE links (
  short_key   CHAR(7) COLLATE "C" PRIMARY KEY,
  long_url    TEXT NOT NULL,
  owner_id    BIGINT,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  expires_at  TIMESTAMP
);
blocks.caption: One row per link. Every read is a lookup by key, using a case-sensitive collation so aZ3kP9q and az3kp9q stay distinct.

blocks.p: Every redirect is a lookup by primary key, and there are no joins on the hot path. A relational database or a key-value store both work. Shard by a hash of the key, as in the sharding lesson. Random keys already spread evenly, so no shard gets more than its share.
Link popularity is very uneven. A link in a viral post gets millions of clicks; most get a handful. That is the shape where a cache works best.

blocks.caption: Creating a link, then two redirects. A cached key answers without touching the database. A miss reads the database and fills the cache. Each click is logged after the redirect is sent, so a crash in between loses that click.
Redirects for 200 links where a few are far more popular. A warm cache holding 40 of them answers over 80% of redirects.

blocks.p: Run the link service in several regions behind DNS that sends users to the nearest one, with a read replica of the database in each. Redirects are read-only, so they keep working even if the primary database is briefly unreachable.

Updating a counter row on every click would turn each redirect into a write, and a viral link into a hot row. Instead, the service appends a click event to an event log. That leaves a choice. Waiting for the log to confirm the event before sending the redirect counts every click, but adds a few milliseconds to each redirect and fails the redirect when the log is down. Sending the redirect first is faster, but a crash between the two loses that click. This design sends the redirect first and treats click counts as close, not exact.

A separate consumer reads the log, counts clicks per key per minute, and writes the totals in batches. Counts lag by a few seconds, which is fine for a dashboard, and the redirect path never waits on them.

list: Estimates show a write load one database handles, and a read load and row count that need a cache and sharding.
Keys are 7 random base62 characters, made unique by the database's key constraint.
Redirects use 302 with `Cache-Control: no-store` so clicks come back to the service, and a cache answers most of them.
Clicks go to an event log and are counted in batches. Logging after the redirect is fast but can lose a click in a crash.
